subject: geography
title: Migration and Urbanisation
welcome_lead: From rural villages to megacities, study why people move and how the world becomes more urban.
meta_desc: Geography Adventure: migration, push-pull factors and global urbanisation.
final_note: You have followed migrants across continents and into cities. Movement remains a defining feature of the 21st century.

concepts.def: Negative conditions encouraging people to leave an origin: conflict, poverty, environmental degradation.
Positive conditions attracting people to a destination: jobs, schools, safety.
Movement of people within a country, especially rural-urban migration.
Movement of people across national borders, voluntary or forced.
Money sent home by migrants, a major source of foreign exchange for many LICs.
Increase in the proportion of population living in urban areas, now over 55% globally.

walkthroughs.body_html: Lee's model (1966) frames migration as the interaction of push factors at origin, pull factors at destination and intervening obstacles (distance, cost, regulation). Stouffer's intervening opportunities model suggests migrants travel only as far as needed to find suitable destinations.

Rural-urban migration drives urbanisation in LICs and MICs. Major international corridors include Mexico-USA, Bangladesh-India, Syria-Turkey, Venezuela-Colombia and movements within the EU. The UN estimates around 280 million international migrants worldwide.

Origins gain remittances but may lose human capital (brain drain). Destinations gain labour but face integration challenges. Urbanisation can drive growth and innovation but also slum expansion, inequality and stress on infrastructure. Climate change is projected to increase environmental migration significantly.

mcqs.q: Why is HDI a better measure of development than GNI per capita?
options: Because HDI is easier to calculate than GNI.
Dependency theory is the same as Rostow's modernisation theory.
HDI combines income, life expectancy and education, capturing quality of life — GNI per capita is just average income and hides inequality and non-economic wellbeing.
Because HDI measures how happy people are.

mcqs.q: How are fold mountains like the Himalayas formed?
options: Dependency theory is the same as Rostow's modernisation theory.
Fold mountains form when one plate slides under another into the mantle.
By the collision of two continental plates (India and Eurasia) where neither can subduct, so the crust crumples and is forced upwards over millions of years.
Fold mountains form from giant volcanoes erupting upwards.

mcqs.q: What does Frank's dependency theory argue?
options: Fold mountains form from giant volcanoes erupting upwards.
Dependency theory says LICs are poor because they depend too much on foreign aid.
That LICs (periphery) are kept poor by exploitative trade relationships with HICs (core) — underdevelopment is actively produced by capitalism, not a stage that countries grow out of.
Dependency theory is the same as Rostow's modernisation theory.
